query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloying of ZrB2 with multiple principal elements can overcome the limitations of single-phase ZrB2 by reducing the required preparation temperature, improving oxidation durability, and enhancing structural integrity in a liquid plating bath.
generation.intervention: High-entropy alloying with multiple principal elements
generation.conditions: Lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength, structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy effect stabilizes the solid-solution phase, reducing the free energy and making the chemically-ordered intermetallic compounds less competitive, resulting in improved properties such as high-temperature stability, strength, and resistance to oxidation and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation durability, enhanced structural integrity, and reduced preparation temperature compared to single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared at high temperatures (>2300 °C)
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and proportions of the high-entropy alloy, as well as the optimal preparation and service conditions, are uncertain and require further research

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-entropy alloyed ZrB2 specimens with varying compositions and proportions, and test their oxidation durability, structural integrity, and mechanical properties at different temperatures and in a liquid plating bath
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloyed ZrB2 specimens do not exhibit improved oxidation durability, structural integrity, and mechanical properties compared to single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, the hypothesis is falsified

The newly-developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are receiving much attention for their unique structures and excellent properties,,,,,,,,,. Unlike traditional alloys, which are normally based on one or two principal elements, HEAs defined by Yeh et al. can have five or more principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios. In recent studies, quaternary and ternary alloys in an equal molar ratio are also considered as HEAs,. The presence of multiple principal elements in HEAs is not merely a difference in composition, but has fundamental physical effects on the configurational entropy, free energy, phase selection, and stability. In general, the high-entropy effect in these alloys can greatly reduce the free energy of simple solid-solution phases, especially at high temperatures, making the chemically-ordered intermetallic compounds less competitive. As a result, HEAs obtained after rapid quenching are often found to contain topologically-simple [e.g., face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC)] yet chemically-disordered solid solutions, nano-sized precipitates, and amorphous phases,,,. Recently, the fabrication and properties of metallic high entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted significant research interests,. In an HEA, the configurational entropy of a solid-solution phase is maximized to stabilize it against the formation of intermetallics. Typically, five or more elements can be mixed in a HEA in equimolar concentrations to produce a maximum molar configurational entropy of ΔSmix = RlnN, where N is the number of equimolar components and R is the gas constant,. “Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature. They are widely used in aviation, aerospace, and automotive and chemical industries, serving in high-temperature (≤ 1100 °C) environments. However, for super high temperature conditions of up to 1500 °C and 3000 °C, traditional surperalloys are powerless. Instead, a new type of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have shown their advantages. High-entropy alloys or multi-element alloys are loosely defined as solid-solution alloys that contain more than five principal elements in equal or near equal atomic percent (at%) [,,]. According to the cocktail effects of HEAs, the alloy properties can be adjusted by composition changes and via alloying [,,]. Materials used in the extreme working environments such as high temperatures or pressures are in an urgent need for industrial application. For example, to improve the efficiency of gas turbine engines in the aerospace industry, increasing engine operating temperature is one of the most effective ways. However, the most commonly used high-temperature structural material, nickel-based superalloy, has its own melting point of about 1300 °C, which limits the maximum operating temperature,. Thus, it is very important that the material has a high enough melting point. Distinct from the conventional alloys, based on one main element concept, high-entropy alloys are composed of five or more principal elements, so they are considered a new class of metallic materials with a different synthesis strategy []. The microstructure and properties of high-entropy alloys [] are influenced by many factors, including the four core effects: The interference between the high entropy effect and complex phase formation (thermodynamics); the sluggish diffusion effect has the potential of slowing down the phase transformation (kinetics); the severe lattice distortion effect can modify the properties to an extent (structure); and the cocktail effect produces surplus to the amount anticipated by the alloying rule, because of the interactions between atoms and severe lattice distortion (properties) [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements in (nearly) equimolar proportions [,] have attracted much attention recently because the unconventional alloying approach results in excellent mechanical properties and surface degradation resistance [,,,,,]. Most of the reported HEA systems have a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) or face-centered cubic (FCC) structure [,,]. To achieve a good balance of high strength of BCC HEAs along with good ductility of FCC HEAs, eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) consisting of the dual phases in lamellar microstructure have been recently developed [,]. Some examples of EHEAs with excellent combination of strength and ductility include CoCrFeNiZr0.5, CoCrFeNiMnPd1.4, CoCrFeNiMnPd0.6, Nb25Sc25Ti25Zr25, AlCrFeNiMo0.2, Al1.2CrCuFeNi2 and AlCoCrFeNix []. In particular, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with lamellar arrangement of BCC (B2) and FCC (L12) solid-solution phases has shown the most promising mechanical properties [,,,]. decision.trend: The trend in the research is to develop high-entropy alloys and ceramics with improved properties, such as high-temperature stability, strength, and resistance to oxidation and corrosion. Earlier studies focused on fabricating high-entropy alloys using various methods, including mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, and laser cladding. Recent studies have explored the use of liquid phase methods to synthesize high-entropy ceramic powders and the development of refractory high-entropy alloys with low activation and high entropy.

The current research has not yet found a single intervention that can overcome these limitations, and further studies are needed to develop a material that meets the required properties.
decision.why: The next step is to explore the use of high-entropy alloying to develop a material that can overcome the limitations of single-phase ZrB2. This approach has shown promise in recent studies, where high-entropy alloys have been developed with improved properties, such as high-temperature stability and resistance to oxidation and corrosion. By introducing multiple principal elements in equal or near-equal proportions, high-entropy alloying can create a material with a single-phase solid solution structure, which can improve its properties and performance.
